Siyona Dubey

Theoretical Physics Researcher & Aerospace Systems Developer

Siyona is an independent theoretical physics researcher and youth advocate specializing in cosmological perturbation theory, cyclic universe mechanics, and high-power aerodynamic modelling. Founder of the Youth Assembly platform and Global Ambassador for educational equity, I focus on open-data simulation, mission telemetry design, and background-independent modeling.
summary: Earth Detective is an interactive web-based platform used to monitor climate change using 40 years of open-source NASA POWER reanalysis data (1985-2024) and NASA GIBS imagery. The tool tracks the urban and megacity heat of 100 cities across the globe. A zero backend tool was created meaning that all the complex statistical analysis was done on the client side. This includes Mann-Kendall trend testing with Sen's Slope, lag-1 autocorrelation and false discovery rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) corrections. The user can view a 3D globe in WebGL showing different sensor views. Satellite telemetry data can also be viewed in real time as well as NASA GIBS land surface temperature and night light data. There is a detailed case file for each city with charts, 2035 heat projections, data source information and the ability to quickly download the data in CSV format. By highlighting heat in the long term at night and urban heat islands the complex and fragmented information can be made simple. This provides insight and makes the data easily accessible for public health and urban planning.
details: Earth Detective is a web based interactive climate monitoring dashboard which was created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. This dashboard uses 40 years worth of NASA data from 100 different cities around the world to determine heat patterns and megacity warming. The dashboard has no backend and uses the frontend to process the current NASA POWER data analysis and NASA GIBS imagery. A powerful statistical analysis has been implemented to ensure accurate data from the climate by using the Mann-Kendall test, Sen's Slope, Lag-1 Autocorrelation and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. There are many benefits to using this dashboard including converting the complex NetCDF data into simple cases, projecting heat exposure for the year 2035, showing sensor locations and exporting to CSV. The goal of this dashboard is to show the constant heating during the night and urban heat islands that can affect public health and infrastructure. It uses HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript and Three.js to create a fun and engaging experience which takes dry scientific data and turns it into a spy satellite dashboard with 5 different sensor modes. The team also thought carefully about making sure the data was accurate by using correct statistics to reduce the chance of false discoveries, making sure the frontend can handle the data and ensuring the dashboard can work without internet by using local caching and fake modes.
